_strings.@@7a926f0e12aa: Treaty conformity — ID conforms to federal treaty treatment — income exempt from federal tax under a treaty is also excluded from ID income (it flows through the federal starting point; do not add it back on the ID return). (This is about TREATY conformity only — a state can conform on treaties while DECOUPLING from the federal Code for deductions or credits; see any law-change lines below.) State note: Idaho's resident return (Form 40) starts on line 7 from federal adjusted gross income ('Enter your federal adjusted gross income from federal Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 11'), and the only statutory additions are on Form 39R, Part A (2025 instructions): federal NOL deduction, capital loss carryover incurred outside the state before becoming an Idaho resident, non-Idaho state/local bond interest and dividends, Idaho college savings account (IDeal) withdrawal, bonus depreciation, and other additions. There is NO add-back of federally treaty-exempt income (unlike CA's Schedule CA). Because treaty-exempt income is already excluded from federal AGI and is not added back, it flows through untaxed. Idaho also affirmatively confirms this in its Noncitizens guidance (re-fetched live this session): 'Idaho honors all tax treaties recognized by the United States' and 'Gross income amounts exempt by treaty are not included in the gross income filing requirement for Idaho' (with a worked Venezuela-treaty example against the $2,500 nonresident threshold). Therefore Idaho conforms to federal treaty exemptions.

This op computes the state's rate-schedule tax line ONLY — county/city add-on taxes, state credits, and any amounts outside the rate schedule are NOT modeled. Pack notes: 2025 CHANGE — RATE CUT AND RE-INDEXED FLOOR: 'Effective January 1, 2025, the individual income tax rate is 5.3%' (What's New for 2025) — down from 2024's 5.695%, enacted by 2025 House Bill 40 — and the Line 20 worksheet's zero-floor subtraction amounts were re-indexed to $4,811 (single/MFS) and $9,622 (MFJ/HOH/QSS), from 2024's $4,673/$9,346. Do not use the 2024 rate or amounts for 2025. The live tax.idaho.gov online guide states the same rate independently of the booklet. 2025 CHANGE — IRC CONFORMITY AND THE STANDARD DEDUCTION: the booklet's What's New says 'Idaho conforms to the IRC as of January 1, 2026' (2024's booklet said January 1, 2024), with bonus depreciation, Idaho net operating losses, and the Idaho Research Credit as notable exceptions. That later conformity date is why the shipped standard deduction is the OBBBA-amended federal 2025 amount — $15,750 single/MFS, $31,500 MFJ/QSS, $23,625 HOH — and NOT the pre-OBBBA inflation-only figures. The age-65/blind additional deduction is likewise $1,600 ($2,000 if single or head of household). Base guidance: Supply Form 40, line 11 'Total Adjusted Income' = federal AGI (Form 40 line 7, from federal Form 1040/1040-SR line 11) plus Form 39R Part A additions minus Form 39R Part B subtractions. With no Idaho additions or subtractions this equals federal AGI. The op subtracts only the per-status standard deduction (Form 40 line 16); if you claim the federal qualified business income deduction (Form 40 line 18) or itemize (Form 40 lines 13-15), the op will overstate tax — subtract your line 18 QBI amount from line 11 before supplying it, or compute on the form. Structure: Idaho's 2025 tax is a single 5.3% rate on Idaho taxable income ABOVE a filing-status threshold — $4,811 (single or married filing separately) / $9,622 (married filing jointly, head of household, or qualifying surviving spouse) — per the Form 40 line 20 worksheet (2025 instructions p.9). It is modeled here as a 0% bracket up to the threshold and 5.3% above it; taxable income at or below the threshold owes $0. Head of household uses the SAME $9,622 worksheet threshold as married filing jointly (instructions p.9), even though its standard deduction ($23,625) differs from MFJ's ($31,500). Qualifying surviving spouse (Form 40 filing status 5) is listed in the worksheet with the same $9,622 amount as married filing jointly, so the engine's QSS-to-MFJ mapping is exact for both the brackets and the $31,500 standard deduction. The worksheet's line 5 prints an explicit zero clause — 'If zero or less, enter zero'; the 0% floor bracket implements the $0 result for taxable income at or below the subtraction amount. Qualified business income deduction NOT modeled: Form 40 line 18 subtracts the federal QBI deduction AFTER the standard/itemized deduction to reach Idaho taxable income (line 19). See base guidance for how to account for it. Itemizers NOT modeled: Form 40 lines 13-15 use federal Schedule A itemized deductions MINUS state and local income or general sales taxes (line 14 addback), so 'it might be more beneficial to itemize for federal purposes but use the standard deduction for Idaho'; filers use the LARGER of net itemized (line 15) or the standard deduction (line 16). The op applies only the standard deduction. Standard-deduction gates NOT modeled (Standard Deduction Worksheet and 'You Must Itemize If', 2025 instructions p.8): married filing separately MUST itemize if the spouse itemizes; a filer with dual status as a nonresident alien for part of 2025 must itemize; a person claimable as another's dependent is limited to the greater of $1,350 or earned income + $450 when earned income exceeds $900 (capped at the status amount); age-65+/blind boxes add $1,600 per box ($2,000 if single or head of household). Compute those cases on the worksheet. Idaho has NO personal or dependent exemptions ('Idaho conforms to the Internal Revenue Code (IRC), which no longer allows personal exemptions' — Noncitizens guidance). The per-person amounts on the return are TAX CREDITS subtracted from tax or refundable payments, not base reductions, and are not modeled: the Idaho Child Tax Credit is $205 per qualifying child age 16 or under (Form 40 line 24 for 2025 — line 25 in 2024, nonrefundable), and the Food Tax Credit (formerly the Grocery Credit) is $155 per qualifying person, or actual Idaho food sales tax up to $250 each with receipts (Form 40 line 43, refundable). $10 Permanent Building Fund (PBF) tax (Form 40 line 31 for 2025 — line 32 in 2024) is a separate flat tax owed by everyone Idaho requires to file an Idaho return (waived for those below the filing threshold — draw a line through the $10 and enter 'NRF' — and for recipients of Idaho public assistance). It is outside the line 20 computation and NOT modeled. New for 2025 and NOT modeled: the Parental Choice Tax Credit (Form 40 line 42), claimable only in the amount pre-approved through Idaho's Taxpayer Access Point; it sits in the Payments and Other Credits section, outside the line 20 tax computation. No tax-table mandate: the 2025 booklet contains no tax tables — every filer computes line 20 with the worksheet, so bracket math reproduces the form exactly (whole-dollar rounding aside). Part-year residents and nonresidents file Form 43, not Form 40; Form 43 line 42 uses the identical worksheet (same $4,811/$9,622 amounts, same 5.3%) applied to Form 43 line 41 Idaho taxable income (2025 instructions p.20).
